Cliff Sosin on the limits of intelligence:

"Superintelligence arrived. You probably didn't notice, because it turned out to be kind of incremental.

I think we overrated intelligence, or misread what it is. 

We hold a thin scatter of facts about the world, and intelligence or reasoning is whatever fills the space between them.

Where the space between the facts behaves well, this is close to godlike. Most of what matters doesn't behave like that. 

The universe is mostly the emergent behavior of complex systems. Stir cream into coffee. Watch a storm build out of nothing but atmospheric temperature differences and water vapor. 

You have to run the thing.

The takeoff story assumed the limit was thinking. It isn't. The limit is contact with reality. 

A smarter reasoner fills the gaps between known facts in simple areas faster and better, but it doesn’t produce new facts.

An AI will hand you a genuinely clever design for a jet turbine blade. It might be far more likely to work than anything your engineers came up with. 

It'll still probably fail, because that’s the base rate at the edge of what anyone knows. The only way to find out is to build the blade and try to break it.

That's the real limit on learning, and it doesn't care how smart you are. Coming up with ideas was never the hard part. The hard part is how fast reality answers them.

Most problems can't be worked out at a desk by thinking. Those stay bound by how fast we can build the thing and see if it holds, and that clock barely moves."

From his essay "Maybe Intelligence Ain't All That." He walks through it here.

Cliff Sosin on why you want to own the complements to cheap intelligence, like Meta does:

"I've found it helpful to assume everyone has really great intelligence and ask what's left. 

If intelligence becomes cheap and ubiquitous, what you want to own are the complements to intelligence. 

The complements are data, attention, love, physical proximity, scale, regulatory capture.

Let's talk about Meta. They have $250 billion of revenue, and they spend $250 billion a year. The question you might ask is, what do they spend it on? A really reductionist view is that they spend it all on intelligence.

They're buying data centers. They're literally buying inference. They're paying really smart people to write algorithms. They're writing code. That's just intelligence.

If you think forward with the fact that the price of intelligence is falling by a factor of a hundred or something over the next five years, their costs kind of go away.

Maybe instead of taking their cost to zero with much better intelligence at much lower prices, maybe they can sell a few more ads.

All of this is downstream of what they possess, which is not destroyed by ubiquitous intelligence, which is data and attention. 

I don't think that the availability of cheap and ubiquitous intelligence is gonna cause people not to be interested in watching funny 20-second videos."

Note: using Oct 1-2 as typically it takes at least five days for dark transits across the SoH to become clear.

Your wallet history, old posts & location clues become far more revealing when machines can connect them into a detailed profile at a speed and scale no human could match

@USDDecentralize has spent years building an ecosystem around two things: earning yield & making stablecoin transfers cheaper.

USDD's Smart Allocator puts reserves to work across blue-chip protocols like @aave, @sparkfinance, and @Morpho, earning interest from borrowers and additional protocol rewards.

Yield gives users a reason to hold USDD, while cheaper transfers make it useful beyond simply sitting in a wallet.

That's a more interesting growth model than attracting deposits with high APYs alone.

Since its expansion from TRON to Ethereum, Ethereum now accounts for 26% of USDD's supply, which gives it another substantial market to attract stablecoin holders beyond TRON's ecosystem.

Definitely a top contender for the top stablecoin spot as a decentralized alternative to Tether and Circle.

Institutions want their own rules inside Ethereum blocks.

A normal transaction on Ethereum is visible to everyone before it is included. That has pushed many institutions onto private chains with far less liquidity.

@ETHGasOfficial lets them book space in Ethereum blocks ahead of time. Transactions sent this way skip the public mempool and are screened against the institution’s own sanctions rules first. Each institution stays in control of its transactions without leaving Ethereum.

Being seen early is expensive for a fund moving a large position. Traders watching the public mempool can spot the trade and buy first, which pushes up the price the fund pays. With reserved blockspace, the fund can buy a whole block and decide what goes ahead of its trade.

Institutions do not have to leave Ethereum for a private chain to set their own rules.

The nuclear renaissance needs fuel. And WHERE that fuel comes from matters increasingly.

The World Nuclear Association’s reference scenario sees annual uranium requirements rising from roughly 69,000 tonnes in 2025 to more than 150,000 tonnes by 2040. Meanwhile, existing mines face depletion.

That means the industry must replace declining production while developing enough new supply to meet growing demand.

America’s challenge is particularly striking: U.S. uranium concentrate production totalled just 2.1 million pounds in 2025, versus utility purchases of 46.9 million pounds. Around 93% of deliveries were foreign-origin.

This is why I see Myriad Uranium as a potential part of the longer-term solution. 

📍 COPPER MOUNTAIN, WYOMING

Myriad owns 100% of a district with extensive historical drilling, past production and multiple uranium deposits. Historic endowment of 655 Mlbs. Phase II drilling is advancing the work towards a maiden modern resource.

Its location brings practical advantages: regional rail, highway and power lines are within 5 km. Infrastructure access matters when trying to turn mineralisation into an economically viable mine.

September’s initial DISA processing tests also offered encouragement: approximately 84% of the uranium was concentrated into just 29% of the sample mass. Reducing the material needing further processing could improve development economics, subject to larger-scale testing.

📍 ARIZONA

On October 7, Myriad regained full control of 24 breccia pipe prospects in the same geological district as Energy Fuels’ Pinyon Plain mine.

That offers another route to exploring for domestic uranium, including historically identified high-grade mineralisation. Pinyon Plain demonstrates what this deposit type can deliver, although Myriad must prove its own targets.

📍 ARGENTINA

The proposed Los Altares acquisition adds approximately 55,000 hectares in the Cerro Solo uranium district, where Argentina is pursuing domestic fuel security.

It broadens Myriad’s exploration opportunity, although the acquisition remains subject to closing and potential ISR suitability is unproven.

My thesis: future uranium supply needs investment today. Projects with geological potential, infrastructure access and strategic relevance deserve attention well before production begins.

More reactors require more fuel. Domestic uranium development could give America greater control over its supply.

Summing up the challenge of commercializing robots in one photo

The bar for both reliability and output quality is much higher for physical labor than it is for knowledge work. A chatbot that produces work that is just “good enough” or low quality can still be useful. 

A mediocre rough draft could still save time because a person can keep what’s good and fix the rest before its final. Copywriting, slides, and contracts can all be edited.

What is considered “good enough” for physical work has much higher standards. A bad weld can ruin metal. A wrong dose given to a patient is unacceptable.

Outputs from work done by humans or robots in the physical often serve as direct inputs into the workflow that are hard to recover from if an error arises. Outputs from work done by humans or Chatbots for knowledge work are much more tolerant of errors and poor quality because supervision can be baked in before the output is used further down the workflow.

The reliability threshold is 2-4 orders of magnitude greater for physical work than knowledge work and it’s what we’ve started to achieve this year. The upside is that by optimizing for reliability, robots will be able to work at a high level of utilization and operate at higher levels of autonomy compared to general purpose AI models in 2023. Machines that can deliver up to 24 hours of work a day as opposed to minutes or hours of work.

NEW FOUNDER ARCHETYPES IN THE AI AGE

Solo founders
- Why: Solo founders can do 100x with AI, so they can ship a v1 when previously they couldn’t have before
- Why not: Maybe a team of cofounders still makes more progress. Maybe you can agentically code but someone still needs to do a million meetings with customers. Maybe coding was never the main bottleneck for startups in the first place?

Non-technical founders
- Why: There’s elite talent that comes from areas like finance, consulting, who can’t code but are passionate about business. There’s also folks in creative industries who create all day but just not in code. Now they can build
- Why not: Why not: Maybe AI makes it easier to build a prototype, but there’s still a big gap between a demo and a reliable product that can scale. If everyone can build the first version, maybe technical judgment becomes more important in deciding what to build, what’s actually possible, and how to stay ahead as the product gets more complex. (especially true for product categories like dev tools/etc)

Domain experts
- Why: A doctor who works at a hospital understands all the problems they face each day. A real estate broker really gets the subtleties of their markets, their clients. Same with a soldier, teacher, etc. What if they could use software to solve their own problems and build business along the way?
- Why not: Hoteliers didn’t create Airbnb and the finance industry didn’t create Kalshi. Sometimes you just need an outsider’s view in order to reinvent an industry, versus building incremental improvements

Kids, high schoolers, college students
- Why: Young people have already been building products early on. Start with a Minecraft mod, a Roblox game, a Discord bot, and suddenly you’ve learned how to make something that thousands of other people use. Now add AI, and a kid with an idea can build way more, way earlier
- Why not: Building something your friends love is very different from building a company. You still have to hire, raise money, manage people, and figure out how to make money. And maybe young founders have an advantage in consumer products because they understand their peers, but much less of one when it comes to enterprise software, healthcare, or other industries where experience and relationships really matter. Sometimes you just need domain expertise

Content creators
- Why: They’re already creating. So instead of creating videos, maybe the same skills can go into creating software. Plus, they have distribution. They know what their followers care about, how to get their attention, and how to reach them without paying for ads. In the past, turning that audience into a software product meant finding a technical cofounder or hiring a team. Now a creator could build and launch something themselves, and immediately put it in front of millions of potential users.
- Why not: Having followers helps with a spike of distribution, but building a sustainable growth engine is something else. The most valuable products aren’t memes - they are long-running, long-growing products that need to be endlessly tweaked and iterated on. Does the DNA work?

gm gm here we go again.

This morning somebody abused a bug in ApeStr to swap 21 apes for 21 ApeStr-owned apes.

This was a known exploit (see the SQUIGSTR exploit from ~1 year ago) but incentive to run it was never there.

The bug lies in buyTargetNFT: it forces a strategy contract to send arbitrary calldata to any target. Afterwards it checks only three things: its BAYC balance rose by exactly 1, it owns expectedId, and "cost" equals its ETH balance drop.

This was patched in later NFTStrategy releases, but affects the original 6 (PunkSTR not affected).

The attacker bought 2 BAYC to use as bait. Using a helper contract, they prep the strategy contract by selling an ape to it for 5 wei and immediately buying it back for 6 wei. That primes the contract's ethToTwap with 6 wei.

They then call buyTargetNFT and pass the calldata to transfer an ape from ApeSTR to the helper using safeTransferFrom. This in turn hands execution over to the helper (remember, safeTransferFrom is NOT safe), which transfer TWO apes back to ApeSTR to satisfy the balance check (1 out, 2 in leaves ApeSTR at +1). It also calls processTokenTwap, which converts the 6 wei, setting the cost of one of the newly deposited apes to 7 wei (6 * 120%). The helper contract buys it back in the same tx.

example flow: 
- Attacker has BAYC #1 and #2. ApeSTR has BAYC #3. 
- Attacker "sells" BAYC #1 to ApeSTR for 6 wei and sends BAYC #2 to it for free, but steals BAYC #3 in the process.
- ApeSTR relists BAYC #1 for 7 wei, which the attacker buys.
- Attacker now has BAYC #1 and BAYC #3, and ApeSTR has BAYC #2 (but doesn't even know it).

The attacker ran this for all 21 BAYC in the ApeSTR contract, resulting in them being able to claim packs for all of those BAYC. Total net proceeds: $14k.

This previously affected SQUIGSTR because of their shared contract - any art blocks NFT sent in would satisfy the balance check, allowing the attacker to drain the contract of squiggles in exchange for basically valueless art blocks NFTs.

It was known to be possible on ApeSTR as well, so I guess it was just a matter of time before we saw it happen.

The unfortunate consequence is that now, ApeSTR has 21 apes that it is completely unaware of, so they cannot be bought from the contract. And 210 attacker-owned mudwater packs were dumped into bids.
